extracted.intended_audience: Cochrane review authors, information specialists, and health/medical librarians involved in intervention systematic reviews
extracted.subtask_short: conducting database searches for Cochrane reviews
extracted.subtask_description: Designing, executing, peer-reviewing and documenting literature searches for Cochrane intervention systematic reviews, including decisions about language, date and format limits, filters, alerts, rerunning searches, and identification of problematic publications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include non-English studies / avoid language restriction
rubrics_metrics.description: Cochrane author teams should plan at the protocol stage not to restrict the search by language and to consider searching databases and trials registers published in languages other than English.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When resources/time allow include studies published in languages other than English to minimise language/indexing bias. If translation or data extraction is needed, seek assistance (e.g. via Cochrane Engage). If it is not possible to extract information from non‑English reports, add such reports to 'studies awaiting classification' (not 'excluded studies') and reflect this in the PRISMA flow diagram or in the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justify and report any date restrictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Date limits may be used to focus searches but the restriction must be reported and justified; date restrictions in the search should only be used when there are date restrictions in the eligibility criteria for studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Date restrictions should only be applied if it is known relevant studies could only have been reported during a specific period (e.g. intervention only available after a certain date). Arbitrary date limits (e.g. 'last 20 years') are not recommended for Cochrane intervention reviews. Provide narrative explanation for date choices and ensure database date fields (create, entry, last update, publication date) and datafile coverage are considered; it may be necessary to search additional datafiles or use a wider date range to account for inconsistent publication dates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid document format restrictions (e.g., letters, comments)
rubrics_metrics.description: Document format restrictions should not be applied to systematic review searches because any information about an eligible study may be valuable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not routinely exclude letters or items indexed as 'Comments' without examination, as they can contain important additional information or early warnings of possible future retraction. Publication format restrictions generally should not be used in Cochrane reviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider preprints as potential sources (with caution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Preprints should be considered a potentially relevant source of study evidence, particularly for emerging topics, but including them raises practical challenges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of limited search/download features of preprint archives, reproducibility challenges, and versioning differences between preprints and final publications. Since peer‑reviewed publications may report information missing from preprints, conduct searches prior to manuscript completion for peer‑reviewed references of any included preprint studies and document approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not automatically exclude studies from 'predatory' journals
rubrics_metrics.description: Search limits should not be applied to exclude articles published in presumed 'predatory journals'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The direction of bias from excluding such journals is unclear (they may publish valid null results or biased positive results). Avoid blanket exclusion based on presumed predatory status; assess studies on their content and quality instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: MECIR C35: Restricting database searches (Mandatory)
rubrics_metrics.description: Justify the use of any restrictions in the search strategy on publication date and publication format.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Date restrictions in the search should only be used when there are date restrictions in the eligibility criteria. Publication format restrictions (e.g. exclusion of letters) should generally not be used in Cochrane reviews. For updates, searches might be naturally restricted by date of entry into the database to avoid duplication of effort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and examine retractions, errata, comments and expressions of concern
rubrics_metrics.description: When considering eligibility, review authors should examine any relevant retraction notices and errata; comments and expressions of concern should be considered for integrity issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Search MEDLINE/Embase for latest citation versions when updating reviews. Errata can reveal important limitations or fatal flaws; retractions often arise from misconduct (duplication, plagiarism, fabrication) and can affect inclusion decisions. Guidance and methods to identify problematic publications are in the Technical Supplement; Cochrane has a policy and implementation guidance for managing potentially problematic studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: MECIR C48: Examining errata (Mandatory)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine any relevant retraction statements and errata for information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Errata, retractions and expressions of concern may lead to exclusion of a study from a review or meta-analysis. Ensure these items are retrieved in database searches by downloading appropriate fields together with citation data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use validated search filters where appropriate, but avoid filters in pre‑filtered databases
rubrics_metrics.description: Use specially designed and tested search filters where appropriate (e.g. Cochrane Highly Sensitive Search Strategies for identifying randomized trials in MEDLINE), but do not use filters in pre-filtered databases (e.g. do not use a randomized trial filter in CENTRAL).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess filters for reliability of development, reported performance, and current accuracy given frequent changes in interfaces and indexing. Use available Cochrane MEDLINE and Embase highly sensitive filters, balanced sensitivity/precision filters as appropriate, and consult the ISSG Search Filter Resource and InterTASC site for filter appraisals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Cochrane Highly Sensitive Search Strategies for identifying randomized trials
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply the provided Cochrane Highly Sensitive Search Strategy syntax (MEDLINE PubMed/Ovid; Embase formats) to identify randomized trials in the respective databases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and ready-to-use search blocks are provided (Box 4.4.a–d) with database-specific syntax notes. Adapt the provided lines and combine as instructed; be mindful of animal filters and NOT exclusions (e.g. #9 NOT #10 constructs) as shown in the boxes.

rubrics_metrics.name: When using machine learning classifiers, avoid duplicate study-design filtering
rubrics_metrics.description: If using study-design classifiers or machine learning to identify trials, ensure database searches used to identify studies do not also contain study-design filters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many systematic review software tools include ML classifiers; when using them it is probably best not to include design filters in the database search. Machine classifiers can achieve high sensitivity/precision but are evolving and limited by available gold-standard training sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer review search strategies (recommendation) and report peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Search strategies should be peer reviewed before execution and the peer review process described in the review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use evidence-based checklists (e.g. PRESS) and experienced searchers/information specialists for peer review. Report the peer review process per PRISMA‑S/PRISMA 2020 guidance; for Cochrane reviews, note names/credentials/institutions of search peer reviewers (with permission) in Acknowledgments. Use PRESS to check technical accuracy and that the strategy addresses protocol needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set up and use alerts / literature surveillance
rubrics_metrics.description: Use alerts (saved searches, TOC alerts, SDIs) to monitor emerging literature and trials registers as a supplement to specific searches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Saved strategies in personal database accounts can notify users by email or RSS when new records match. Alerts help monitor topics after initial searches; they can indicate new potentially eligible studies to include immediately or to list under 'studies awaiting classification'. Consider alerts beyond databases (trials registers, regulatory info) and use TOC alerts for broader monitoring.

rubrics_metrics.name: MECIR C37: Rerunning searches near publication (Mandatory)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rerun or update searches for all relevant sources within 12 months before publication of the review or review update, and screen the results for potentially eligible studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If initial search date is more than 12 months (preferably 6 months) from intended publication, rerun searches close to publication and screen results. Ideally incorporate newly identified studies fully; if not feasible, report them at minimum as references under 'Studies awaiting classification' (or 'Ongoing studies').

rubrics_metrics.name: MECIR C38: Incorporating findings from rerun searches (Highly desirable)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fully incorporate any studies identified in the rerun or update of the search within 12 months before publication of the review or review update.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance the decision to incorporate new studies against potential delay to publication. The published review should be as up to date as possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deciding when to stop searching / assessing search completeness
rubrics_metrics.description: Deciding when to stop developing/running searches is iterative; use stopping rules and tests of adequacy rather than arbitrary endpoints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Possible stopping rules: adding new terms yields no new relevant records, or precision falls below a cut-off. Check whether the search finds key publications and records included in similar reviews (but avoid bias towards known studies). Use citation searches and reference checking to assess coverage. Use evidence-based checklists (PRESS) to identify missing dimensions. Consider topic evidence volume: for scarce evidence be more cautious about stopping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use statistical/empirical techniques to assess search performance
rubrics_metrics.description: Techniques such as capture-recapture (capture-mark-recapture) and relative recall can be used to estimate missed studies and to inform stopping decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Capture-recapture requires results from at least two searches to estimate missed studies and may support iterative searching and selection. Relative recall assesses how many eligible studies indexed in a database were retrieved by the database search; it is most useful at the end of search process. These techniques require further evaluation but may inform decisions about continuing searches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use citation searches and reference checking to validate search performance
rubrics_metrics.description: Citation searches and reference checking can reveal additional relevant studies and act as checks on whether searches have been complete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If citation/reference methods find documents already retrieved by the searches but not previously recognized, this suggests adequate performance. If they find many records missed by database searches, then the strategy may be suboptimal and require revision.
